videos.title: Democrats Sweep in Midterm GOP Implosion
videos.description:
Democrats swept into power in Congress on Tuesday, with outrage over the cost of living and the war in Iran leading to a thundering rebuke of President Donald Trump and his party just two years after his dominant White House comeback. Bloomberg's Josh Wingrove reports from Washington. Data center developers in Texas are facing their worst-case scenario under a newly elected Democratic governor. Bloomberg News Tech Reporter Brody Ford explains. Wall Street strategists are warning that the return of divided government could disrupt the bond market next year by setting the stage for a bruising fight over the debt ceiling. We hear from Maya MacGuineas of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Plus - the prediction market industry had a strong election night performance of its own. We speak with Nicole Kagan, Researcher at Kalshi. All on the latest edition of Bloomberg Businessweek Daily.

videos.title: Can France Still Afford Its Generous Welfare State?
videos.description:
France is on the edge of a financial spiral. The global surge in interest rates has exposed the country, once considered an oasis of stability in Europe’s financial markets, as one of the continent’s weakest links. France now pays more to borrow than former crisis hot spots like Greece and Italy. With government debt growing faster than the economy, the pressure on France to rein in its budget deficit has never been higher. CNBC's Liz Napolitano reports.

videos.title: Why The Midterms May Not Change America’s $40 Trillion Debt
videos.description:
The U.S. national debt has surpassed $40 trillion, while the federal budget deficit for fiscal 2026 reached nearly $2 trillion. CNBC's Matt Peterson and Alex Harring break down what's driving America's growing debt, how rising Treasury yields and interest payments could affect mortgage rates and the broader economy, and whether AI-driven economic growth or action in Washington could help address the country's fiscal challenges.

videos.title: The 'Socialist' Bank Thriving In Trump Country
videos.description:
Progressive political candidates have clamored to launch public banks in the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections. However, there is just one active example in the United States: the Bank of North Dakota. Chartered in 1919, this bank uses tax revenue from the state to fund and execute strategic economic development priorities for North Dakota. The bank has assisted in sales of fossil fuel assets, a presidential library, and general lending to citizens and businesses in need. CNBC's Garrett Downs reports on this “socialist experiment” unfolding deep in Trump country.

videos.title: Why The Measles Outbreak Signals A Bigger Problem In The U.S.
videos.description:
The U.S. is on track to lose its official measles-free elimination status, as cases have soared across the country. Health experts warn that this could be indicative of more problems to come. Vaccination rates for a variety of diseases – that have been largely pushed out of the U.S. – have been falling in recent years. Steeper declines could lead to millions of new cases in the coming years, according to scientific prediction models. Watch the video to learn about what this means for public health.

videos.title: Why Young Airplanes Are Being Torn Apart For Scrap
videos.description:
Some of the world’s most popular commercial airplanes are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected. These aircraft are getting stripped of valuable parts worth millions. The rest is crushed and recycled. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs for years. CNBC went to Goodyear, Arizona to find out why.

videos.title: The Race To Power AI Is Reshaping America's Electric Grid
videos.description:
AI data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and putting renewed pressure on America’s power grid to modernize its equipment and develop greener, more efficient sources of power. Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are all spending millions of dollars on local infrastructure upgrades and companies like SpaceXAI are even building off-grid power plants to power their data centers.

Google says its planned 780-megawatt data center in Pine Island, Minnesota, could offer a model for powering the AI boom. In a proposed agreement with Xcel Energy, Google says it will support 1,900 megawatts of new wind, solar and battery capacity, while minimum payments and exit fees are intended to protect local ratepayers if demand falls short.

CNBC examines whether projects like Pine Island can make the grid cleaner without shifting costs to existing customers, why some energy experts argue that smaller data centers could make better use of infrastructure already in place, and how utilities’ financial incentives can complicate efforts to build less.
